title: Lesson 77: Agent-to-Agent Communication: Protocols, Contracts, and Discovery
description: Choosing the right edge (MCP versus A2A), reading the task lifecycle as the real contract between peers, and treating a discovered Agent Card as a claim from a stranger rather than a guarantee.

questions.question: Your team needs an agent to obtain a verdict from another team's autonomous agent that runs its own planning loop. Per the lesson, which boundary are you crossing and why does it matter?
options: An agent boundary, so the peer belongs behind A2A where the task id, cancellation, partial artifacts, and input requests survive; wrapping it as an MCP tool discards exactly those
A tool boundary, so MCP is correct because every remote capability should be exposed as a callable function
Either protocol works identically because both use JSON-RPC 2.0, so pick the one with fewer dependencies
An agent boundary, so the client should import the peer's prompt and tool definitions to keep behavior consistent
questions.explanation: The lesson separates the two edges: MCP standardizes reaching tools and data, while A2A exists for independent, opaque agents and preserves the durable task, cancellation, artifacts, and input requests. Wrapping an agent as a tool throws those away.

questions.question: A client submits a task and the peer returns TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED. According to the lesson, what is the correct client behavior?
options: Treat it as a failure and open a new task with a fresh messageId
Poll GetTask without limit until the state changes to completed
Treat it as an interrupted state, supply the missing information in another message bound to the same task id, and keep the context
Cancel the task and retry the whole request later with a different payload
questions.explanation: INPUT_REQUIRED and AUTH_REQUIRED are interrupted states, not terminal ones. The lesson warns that clients handling only completed and failed will strand work that was waiting on one clarification, and that resending as new work loses the task continuity.

questions.question: An agent discovers a peer through a well-known Agent Card and reads its skill description and examples into its own context. Which stance does the lesson prescribe?
options: The card is authoritative, so a declared capability is enough authorization to delegate whatever the description claims
A valid JWS signature proves the peer is trustworthy and its outputs can skip downstream validation
The card body can be ignored at runtime because versions change too often to check capabilities
The card is provider-controlled text and a claim: check capabilities and version at runtime, decide delegation from your own policy, and treat the descriptions as untrusted data
questions.explanation: The lesson calls the card an advertisement written by the party asking for work, notes that skill names, descriptions, and examples are free-form remote text entering a prompt, and states that signature verification answers origin only, not trustworthiness or accuracy.
